In the provided historical framing, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution are presented as stages in an evolving effort to create an effective national government for the United States.

The source portrays the Articles as emerging directly from the struggle for independence: “The united efforts to establish independence gave birth to the Articles of Confederation, which though inadequate, were a real step toward the "more perfect Union" of the Constitution.” In this account, the Articles represented a first attempt at union—a “League of Friendship” among sovereign states—rather than a strong national system.

Financially, “It had no means of revenue independent of that received through its requisitions on the States, which were nothing more than requests, which the States could and did disregard;” so the central authority could not reliably raise money. Economically, “it had no control over foreign or interstate commerce.” More broadly, “It had responsibility but no power as a national government; no means of coercing the States to obedience even to the very inadequate grant given to the "League of Friendship" by the Articles of Confederation.”

The source also emphasizes a deeper structural problem about where authority came from. It states that “its greatest weakness was that it had no direct origin in, or action on, the people themselves; but, unlike both the Declaration of Independence and the later Constitution, knew only the States and was known only to them, calling them sovereign.” In this narrative, the Articles are contrasted with the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution as lacking direct grounding in “the people” and operating only through state governments.

Within this interpretive framework, the Constitution was created to move beyond a loose league of sovereign states and to form a stronger, more directly popular national government—a “more perfect Union” that corrected the Articles’ lack of revenue power, control over commerce, enforceable national authority, and direct connection to the people.

The source portrays the Articles as emerging directly from the struggle for independence: “The united efforts to establish independence gave birth to the Articles of Confederation, which though inadequate, were a real step toward the "more perfect Union" of the Constitution.” In this account, the Articles represented a first attempt at union—a “League of Friendship” among sovereign states—rather than a strong national system.

Several weaknesses of the Articles are highlighted as reasons a new constitutional framework was needed. Financially, “It had no means of revenue independent of that received through its requisitions on the States, which were nothing more than requests, which the States could and did disregard;” so the central authority could not reliably raise money. Economically, “and it had no control over foreign or interstate commerce.” More broadly, “It had responsibility but no power as a national government; no means of coercing the States to obedience even to the very inadequate grant given to the "League of Friendship" by the Articles of Confederation.”

The source also emphasizes a deeper structural problem about where authority came from. It states that “its greatest weakness was that it had no direct origin in, or action on, the people themselves; but, unlike both the Declaration of Independence and the later Constitution, knew only the States and was known only to them, calling them sovereign.” In this narrative, the Articles are contrasted with the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution as lacking direct grounding in “the people” and operating only through state governments.

Within this interpretive framework, the Constitution was created to move beyond a loose league of sovereign states and to form a stronger, more directly popular national government—a “more perfect Union” that corrected the Articles’ lack of revenue power, control over commerce, enforceable national authority, and direct connection to the people.
